newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican village sees troubled history repeated.
newsitem.headline: Mexican village sees troubled history repeated.

text.p: As troops fought pitched battles with leftist rebels here this week, residents of this remote Mexican village watched history repeat itself.

Twenty years earlier, soldiers swept through this area in search of a rag-tag army of leftist guerrillas who were eventually wiped out but served as inspiration to today's Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) rebels.
"It's the same thing all over again, the soldiers, the bullets flying through the air, the anti-government rebels," Raymundo Pano Juarez, an 80-year old bean farmer in the area, told Reuters.

Marxist EPR rebels and the army clashed on Tuesday a few miles (kilometers) down a dusty road from El Guanabano, but an estimated 20 armed rebels retreated through the village toward the nearby thicket of dry bush and vanished.
At least five people died in the fighting and several others were wounded.

Troops with M-16 automatic rifles and armoured vehicles followed the rebels, keeping nervous eyes on the nearby hills for signs of the group which has vowed to topple the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.

The EPR emerged a year ago in the dirt-poor areas of central and western Guerrero, the same mountainous region where Lucio Cabanas Barrientos and Genaro Vasquez Rojas, two rural teachers, formed rebel armies in the 1970s.
Little has changed in that time. The inaccessible mountains are an hour by car from the glitzy Pacific resort of Acapulco. However, they are centuries away in terms of development.
There is no running water or electricity and almost no one can read.
And for residents of El Guanabano, soldiers chasing rebels are a familiar sight.

Many villages here were targets of a dirty war by the army in the 1970s against Cabanas and Vasquez -- whose supporters numbered in the hundreds but whose fame made them folk legends across Mexico. Cabanas was killed in 1974.
One local woman, who did not want to be identified, said two of her cousins joined Cabanas' rebels in the 1970s and were tortured and killed by the army.

Although not on the scale of repression in neighbouring Central America, the army was said to have used torture and disappearances to wipe out hot spots of rebel support. Some say a similar campaign is underway again against the EPR.

"These areas had conflicts with the army in the 1970s and the memory of that still lives," said Javier Galeana Cadena, a member of Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and mayor of nearby Atoyac de Alvarez.
"When I campaigned there last year, I got almost no welcome. We won 15 votes compared to hundreds for the opposition," Galeana said.
Galeana said he wanted to change all that and planned to bring electricity and running water to several communities.

A few days before Tuesday's battle, Galeana spent three days in the area resolving a dispute between local teachers and used the opportunity to hand out free gifts to local children -- a move which won him some support among locals.
Mexico's leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) claimed this week that several of its supporters in Guerrero had been arrested following recent EPR clashes with the army.
Local members of a dissident teachers' union said several of their activists have gone missing in the past few months -- detained at army roadblocks and never seen again.
El Guanabano residents were eager to tell visiting reporters that although they did not often vote for the long-ruling PRI, they were not guerrilla supporters.
"The first thing the army does is come and point a rifle at you. They ask if you have seen the guerrillas. I offer them coffee and bread," bean farmer Pano said.
"We want no trouble here, just the chance to work the land and make a living," he added.
